intro.title: Ride the line
intro.text: This tour runs a simulated pipeline and stops at every station. At each stop you'll see what a real CI/CD pipeline does there, what to watch for in DeployX, and the classic way that stage breaks.
points: Each station is a pipeline stage. The train is your commit, travelling toward the terminus: the environment it will run in.
The run pauses before every stop. Press Continue to move on, or break a stage to see what a failure looks like.
Everything is simulated. Nothing touches real servers, and tour runs are tagged and kept out of your statistics.

fallback.watch: Watch the log and the station status.
fallback.risk: Any stage can fail, and a failure stops the line so nothing broken moves on.

git.headline: Something changes, the pipeline starts
git.real: A push to the repository fires a webhook. The CI system checks the request really came from the Git host, then queues a run for that exact commit.
git.watch: The first log lines name the commit, the branch and the run ID. Every later stage works on this one commit.
git.risk: A rotated secret or a broken webhook means pushes are rejected or ignored and nothing runs at all.

checkout.headline: Get exactly the code that was pushed
checkout.real: A fresh, clean runner clones the repository and checks out the commit. Starting clean means yesterday's leftovers can't hide a problem.
checkout.watch: The same commit hash is used from here to production. That is what makes the results trustworthy.
checkout.risk: Private submodules or missing permissions: the runner has no person to type a password.

build.headline: Turn source into something deployable
build.real: Dependencies are installed and the code is compiled or bundled into an artifact, often a container image. It is built once and the same artifact is reused in every environment.
build.watch: The image is tagged with the commit hash. That artifact is what gets promoted and rolled back later.
build.risk: Works on my laptop, fails on the runner: case-sensitive file names, missing dependencies, different tool versions.

test.headline: Prove it still works
test.real: Unit tests check small pieces, integration tests check pieces together. They catch regressions before users do, and a failing test stops the line.
test.watch: The log shows test counts and coverage. Failing here costs minutes; failing in production costs customers.
test.risk: Tests that depend on the clock, the timezone or the order they run in pass locally and fail in CI.

security.headline: Check for known holes
security.real: Dependency audits, static analysis and secret scanning look for vulnerabilities and leaked keys. High-severity findings block the release.
security.watch: It often runs in parallel with testing to save time. If one of the two fails, the other is cancelled (fail-fast).
security.risk: A transitive dependency with a known vulnerability, or a key committed by accident.

approval.headline: A human decides
approval.real: Protected environments require sign-off from reviewers before the deploy goes ahead. The author can't approve their own change, so a second pair of eyes always sees it.
approval.watch: Production needs two approvals and has a timeout; Development passes straight through. A rejection or a timeout stops the run without counting as a failure.
approval.risk: Approvals that sit unseen for hours. Waiting is often the biggest part of lead time.

deploy.headline: Roll it out, then verify
deploy.real: The artifact is released with a strategy such as rolling, blue/green or canary. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version first and watches its error rate; if the errors rise, it rolls back on its own. Health checks confirm the new version is serving before the old one is retired.
deploy.watch: Production uses a canary: watch the traffic bar above the Deploy station grow from 10% to 50% to 100%. Break this stage to see an automatic rollback.
deploy.risk: Missing environment config, or a memory limit that is too low: the app starts, dies, and health checks never pass.

lint.headline: Cheap checks first
lint.real: Linters and formatters catch style problems and obvious mistakes in seconds, before slower stages spend minutes.
lint.watch: Fast checks belong early, so failures are cheap.
lint.risk: Rules nobody agrees on turn lint into noise that people learn to ignore.

e2e.headline: Walk the real user journeys
e2e.real: A headless browser clicks through the key flows, such as browse, add to cart and check out, against the built application.
e2e.watch: Slow but realistic. Keep to the few journeys that matter most.
e2e.risk: Timeouts and fragile selectors: the test fails although the app is fine, or the other way round.

license.headline: Check what you're allowed to ship
license.real: Every dependency has a license. The audit checks them against company policy so a restrictive license doesn't slip in unnoticed.
license.watch: It is cheap and can run in parallel with other checks.
license.risk: A new package with a copyleft license pulled in indirectly.

perf.headline: Measure speed before users do
perf.real: A short load test checks response times and error rates against an agreed budget.
perf.watch: A budget such as p95 under 300 ms turns 'feels slow' into a pass or a fail.
perf.risk: A query that is fine with ten rows and terrible with ten million.

migrate.headline: Change the database safely
migrate.real: Schema migrations run before the new version starts. They should also work with the old version, so a rollback stays possible.
migrate.watch: Database changes are the hardest thing to undo.
migrate.risk: Long locks that block live traffic, or a migration that cannot be reversed.

smoke.headline: Confirm the live release works
smoke.real: A few quick requests against the real environment right after the deploy prove the key pages respond.
smoke.watch: If it fails, roll back first and investigate second.
smoke.risk: The deploy is green, but a critical page returns an error.

done.title: You rode the whole line
done.text: The release reached its destination. Here is what the line was doing for you:
points: Fast, cheap checks come first; slower, riskier steps come later.
A failure stops everything after it, so nothing broken moves on.
Protected environments need a second pair of eyes.
DORA metrics turn all of this into numbers: how often you ship, how long it takes, how often it breaks and how fast you recover.

failed.title: The line stopped
failed.text: That is a pipeline doing its job: the problem was caught at {stage} and nothing after it ran. A real team reads the logs, fixes the cause and runs again. The Retry button on the Overview does exactly that, and Incident Drills let you practise finding the fix.
